tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 21
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\bigl|\, |x - 5| - 2\bigr| \le 4$ is $[1, 9]$.
The inequality ${0 < x^{2} - 10x + 25 \le 16}$ has solution set $[1, 5) \cup (5, 9]$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{5x + 1} - \sqrt{2x + 4} > 1$ is $x \ge \frac{4}{3}$.
The solution set of the inequality $|2x - 5| \ge |3x + 1|$ is $[-6, 0.8]$.
The inequality ${2 \le x^{2} + 2x - 1 < 10}$ has solution set $(-1 - 2\sqrt{3}, -3] \cup [1, -1 + 2\sqrt{3})$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The solution set of the inequality $\bigl|\, |x - 5| - 2\bigr| \le 4$ is $[1, 9]$.**  (false)

**First inequality**

$-4 \le |x - 5| - 2 \le 4$, so $-2 \le |x - 5| \le 6$. The left part, $|x - 5| \ge -2$, is automatically true for every x, since an absolute value can never be less than a negative number — it adds no restriction at all. The right part, $|x - 5| \le 6$, gives $-1 \le x \le 11$.

True solution: $[-1, 11]$ — much wider than the $[1, 9]$ stated here.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 0$ (outside the stated $[1, 9]$ but inside the true solution): $\bigl|\, |0-5|-2\bigr| = |5-2| = 3 \le 4$, true — this disproves the narrower stated interval.

**B) The inequality ${0 < x^{2} - 10x + 25 \le 16}$ has solution set $[1, 5) \cup (5, 9]$.**  (true)

**Left part**

$x^{2} - 10x + 25 > 0$

$(x - 5)^{2} > 0$, true for every x except $x = 5$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} - 10x + 25 \le 16$

$x^{2} - 10x + 9 \le 0$

$(x - 1)(x - 9) \le 0$

${1 \le x \le 9}$. 

**Intersection**

$[1, 9]$ with $x = 5$ removed

$[1, 5) \cup (5, 9]$ — matches exactly.

**C) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{5x + 1} - \sqrt{2x + 4} > 1$ is $x \ge \frac{4}{3}$.**  (false)

**Domain**

${5x + 1 \ge 0}$ and ${2x + 4 \ge 0}$, so $x \ge -0.2$. Rewrite as $\sqrt{5x+1} > 1 + \sqrt{2x+4}$. Squaring (right side $\ge$ 1 > 0): ${5x + 1 > 1 + 2\sqrt{2x+4} + (2x+4)}$

${3x - 4 > 2\sqrt{2x+4}}$. The left side must be $\ge$ 0, forcing $x \ge$ $\dfrac{4}{3}$. Squaring again: $(3x - 4)^{2} > 4(2x+4)$

${9x^{2} - 32x > 0}$

$x(9x - 32) > 0$

$x < 0$ or $x >$ $\dfrac{32}{9}$ ≈ 3.56.

**Restrict to case**

Combined with $x \ge$ $\dfrac{4}{3}$, only $x >$ $\dfrac{32}{9}$ survives — a much stricter condition than $x \ge$ $\dfrac{4}{3}$ alone.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 2$ (satisfies $x \ge$ $\dfrac{4}{3}$ but not the true solution): $\sqrt{11} - \sqrt{8} \approx 3.317 - 2.828 = 0.488$, which is not > 1 — disproving the stated answer.

**D) The solution set of the inequality $|2x - 5| \ge |3x + 1|$ is $[-6, 0.8]$.**  (true)

Since both sides are non-negative, squaring preserves the inequality: $(2x - 5)^{2} \ge (3x+1)^{2}$. Expanding: ${4x^{2} - 20x + 25 \ge 9x^{2} + 6x + 1}$

${0 \ge 5x^{2} + 26x - 24}$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = 0.8$ and $x = -6$. Since the parabola opens upward, this quadratic is $\le$ 0 between its roots: $-6 \le x \le 0.8$.

**E) The inequality ${2 \le x^{2} + 2x - 1 < 10}$ has solution set $(-1 - 2\sqrt{3}, -3] \cup [1, -1 + 2\sqrt{3})$.**  (true)

**Left part**

$x^{2} + 2x - 1 \ge 2$

$x^{2} + 2x - 3 \ge 0$

$(x+3)(x - 1) \ge 0$

$x \le -3$ or $x \ge 1$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} + 2x - 1 < 10$

$x^{2} + 2x - 11 < 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = -1 \pm 2\sqrt{3}$, giving $-1 - 2\sqrt{3} < x < -1 + 2\sqrt{3}$. 

**Intersection**

$(-1 - 2\sqrt{3}, -3] \cup [1, -1 + 2\sqrt{3})$ — matches exactly.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 22
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{2x + 9} - \sqrt{x + 5} > 1$ is $x > -1 - 2\sqrt{3}$.
The solution set of the inequality $|x^{2} - 4x - 1| > 4$ is $x < -1$ or ${1 < x < 3}$ or $x > 5$.
The inequality $-6 \le x^{2} - 4x - 3 < 5$ has solution set $(2 - 2\sqrt{3}, 2 + 2\sqrt{3})$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x + 3} < x - 1$ is $x > \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}$.
The solution set of the inequality $|x + 2| + |x - 5| \le 10$ is $[-3.5, 6.5]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{2x + 9} - \sqrt{x + 5} > 1$ is $x > -1 - 2\sqrt{3}$.**  (false)

**Domain**

${2x + 9 \ge 0}$ and $x + 5 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -4.5$. Rewrite as $\sqrt{2x+9} > 1 + \sqrt{x+5}$. Squaring (right side $\ge$ 1 > 0): ${2x + 9 > 1 + 2\sqrt{x+5} + (x+5)}$

$x + 3 > 2\sqrt{x+5}$. The left side must be $\ge$ 0, forcing $x \ge -3$. Squaring again: $(x+3)^{2} > 4(x+5)$

$x^{2} + 2x - 11 > 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = -1 \pm 2\sqrt{3}$. Since the parabola opens upward, it is positive outside the roots; combined with $x \ge -3$, only the larger root matters (since $-1 - 2\sqrt{3} \approx -4.46$ is below -3), giving $x > -1 + 2\sqrt{3} \approx 2.46$ — not the smaller root stated here.

**Quick check:** $-1 + 2\sqrt{3} \approx 2.46$ and $-1 - 2\sqrt{3} \approx -4.46$; since x must already be $\ge$ -3, only the larger root can be the true boundary.

**B) The solution set of the inequality $|x^{2} - 4x - 1| > 4$ is $x < -1$ or ${1 < x < 3}$ or $x > 5$.**  (true)

Let y = $x^{2} - 4x - 1$. The inequality $|y| > 4$ splits into y > 4 or y < -4. Branch y > 4: $x^{2} - 4x - 5 > 0$

$(x - 5)(x+1) > 0$

$x < -1$ or $x > 5$. Branch y < -4: $x^{2} - 4x + 3 < 0$

$(x - 1)(x - 3) < 0$

${1 < x < 3}$. Both branches contribute real solutions, giving the full three-piece answer stated.

**C) The inequality $-6 \le x^{2} - 4x - 3 < 5$ has solution set $(2 - 2\sqrt{3}, 2 + 2\sqrt{3})$.**  (false)

**Left part**

$x^{2} - 4x - 3 \ge -6$

$x^{2} - 4x + 3 \ge 0$

$(x - 1)(x - 3) \ge 0$

$x \le 1$ or $x \ge 3$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} - 4x - 3 < 5$

$x^{2} - 4x - 8 < 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = 2 \pm 2\sqrt{3}$, giving ${2 - 2\sqrt{3} < x < 2 + 2\sqrt{3}}$. 

**Intersection**

$(2 - 2\sqrt{3}, 1] \cup [3, 2 + 2\sqrt{3})$ — two separate pieces, not the single interval stated here.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 2$ (inside the stated interval but not the true solution): 4 - 8 - 3 = -7, and is -6 $\le$ -7? No — this single failing value disproves the stated interval.

**D) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x + 3} < x - 1$ is $x > \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}$.**  (true)

**Domain**

$x + 3 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -3$. **Case 1** — $x - 1 < 0 (x < 1)$: the right side is negative, so a square root (always $\ge$ 0) can never be less than it. No solutions here. **Case 2** — $x - 1 \ge 0 (x \ge 1)$: square safely: $x + 3 < x^{2} - 2x + 1$

$x^{2} - 3x - 2 > 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are x = $\dfrac{3 ± √17}{2}$ ≈ 3.56 and ≈ -0.56. Since the parabola opens upward, it is positive outside its roots; combined with $x \ge 1$, only $x >$ $\dfrac{3+√17}{2}$ survives.

**E) The solution set of the inequality $|x + 2| + |x - 5| \le 10$ is $[-3.5, 6.5]$.**  (true)

The expressions change sign at $x = -2$ and $x = 5$, so split into three regions. $x < -2$: $(-x - 2)+(5-x) = -2x+3 \le 10$ gives $x \ge -3.5$, contributing $[-3.5, -2)$. $-2 \le x \le 5$: $(x+2)+(5-x) = 7$, a constant, and 7 $\le$ 10 always, so the whole region $[-2, 5]$ is included. $x > 5$: $(x+2)+(x - 5) = 2x - 3 \le 10$ gives $x \le 6.5$, contributing $(5, 6.5]$. Combining all three pieces gives $[-3.5, 6.5]$.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 23
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inequality ${0 \le x^{2} - 8x + 12 \le 5}$ has solution set $(1, 2) \cup (6, 7)$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{4x - 3} \ge x - 1$ is $[0.75, 3 + \sqrt{5})$.

The inequality $-3 < x^{2} - 2x - 2 < 6$ has solution set $(-2, 4)$.
tactical_explanations:

**Left part**

$x^{2} - 8x + 12 \ge 0$

$(x - 2)(x - 6) \ge 0$

$x \le 2$ or $x \ge 6$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} - 8x + 12 \le 5$

$x^{2} - 8x + 7 \le 0$

$(x - 1)(x - 7) \le 0$

${1 \le x \le 7}$. 

**Intersection**

$[1, 2] \cup [6, 7]$ — every listed endpoint must be included, since both pieces use non-strict $\le$ / $\ge$ symbols. The stated interval wrongly uses open parentheses.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 2$: 4 - 16 + 12 = 0, and is 0 $\le$ 0 $\le$ 5? Yes — so $x = 2$ must be included, disproving the open interval.

**B) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{4x - 3} \ge x - 1$ is $[0.75, 3 + \sqrt{5})$.**  (false)

**Domain**

${4x - 3 \ge 0}$, so $x \ge 0.75$. **Case 1** — $x - 1 < 0 (x < 1)$: the right side is negative, so the inequality holds automatically. Contributes $[0.75, 1)$. **Case 2** — $x - 1 \ge 0 (x \ge 1)$: square safely: ${4x - 3 \ge x^{2} - 2x + 1}$

$x^{2} - 6x + 4 \le 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = 3 \pm \sqrt{5}$.

**Restrict to case**

Combined with $x \ge 1$: $[1, 3 + \sqrt{5}]$.

**Combine cases**

Union of both cases: $[0.75, 3 + \sqrt{5}]$ — with the upper bound ${3 + \sqrt{5}}$ included, since it comes from a non-strict ( $\ge$ ) condition. The stated half-open interval wrongly excludes it.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 3 + \sqrt{5} \approx 5.236$: $\sqrt{4x - 3} \approx 4.236$, and $x - 1 \approx 4.236$, and is 4.236 $\ge$ 4.236? Yes — so this boundary must be included, disproving the stated open endpoint.

**C) The solution set of the inequality $|4x - 1| > |2x + 7|$ is $x < -1$ or $x > 4$.**  (true)

Since both sides are non-negative, squaring preserves the inequality: $(4x - 1)^{2} > (2x+7)^{2}$. Expanding: ${16x^{2} - 8x + 1 > 4x^{2} + 28x + 49}$

${12x^{2} - 36x - 48 > 0}$. Dividing by 12: $x^{2} - 3x - 4 > 0$, which factors as $(x - 4)(x+1) > 0$, giving $x < -1$ or $x > 4$.

**D) The inequality $-3 < x^{2} - 2x - 2 < 6$ has solution set $(-2, 4)$.**  (false)

**Left part**

$x^{2} - 2x - 2 > -3$

$x^{2} - 2x + 1 > 0$

$(x - 1)^{2} > 0$, true for every x except $x = 1$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} - 2x - 2 < 6$

$x^{2} - 2x - 8 < 0$

$(x - 4)(x+2) < 0$

$-2 < x < 4$. 

**Intersection**

$(-2, 4)$ with $x = 1$ removed

$(-2, 1) \cup (1, 4)$ — the stated $(-2, 4)$ wrongly includes $x = 1$.

**Common trap:** A perfect square that is "strictly greater than 0" always excludes exactly one point — solving the left part as if it allowed equality erases that single gap from the final answer.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 1$ directly: 1 - 2 - 2 = -3, and is -3 > -3? No — so $x = 1$ must be excluded, even though it sits inside $(-2, 4)$.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 24
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x^{2} - 4x - 5} \le x + 2$ is $[\frac{-9}{8}, -1] \cup [5, \infty)$.
The solution set of the inequality $|x - 3| - |x + 1| \ge -2$ is $(-\infty, 2)$.
The inequality ${3 < x^{2} + 2x - 1 < 11}$ has solution set $(-1 - \sqrt{13}, -1 - \sqrt{5}) \cup (-1 + \sqrt{5}, -1 + \sqrt{13})$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x + 3} + \sqrt{x + 8} \le 5$ is $[-3, 1]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x^{2} - 4x - 5} \le x + 2$ is $[\frac{-9}{8}, -1] \cup [5, \infty)$.**  (true)

The square root needs $x^{2} - 4x - 5 \ge 0$. Factor: $(x - 5)(x+1) \ge 0$, giving $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 5$ as the domain. Since a square root is never negative, the right side $x + 2$ must also be $\ge$ 0, forcing $x \ge -2$.

**Restrict to case**

Combined with the domain: $[-2, -1] \cup [5, \infty)$. For x in $[-2, -1]$, square both sides (right side is $\ge$ 0 here): $x^{2} - 4x - 5 \le x^{2} + 4x + 4$

$-9 \le 8x$

$x \ge -$$\dfrac{9}{8}$. So this piece narrows to [-$\dfrac{9}{8}$, -1]. For $x \ge 5$, the same squaring gives $x \ge -$$\dfrac{9}{8}$, which is automatically true, so the whole branch $[5, \infty)$ is valid. Solution: [-$\dfrac{9}{8}$, -1] $\cup$ $[5, \infty)$.

**B) The solution set of the inequality $|x - 3| - |x + 1| \ge -2$ is $(-\infty, 2)$.**  (false)

The expressions change sign at $x = -1$ and $x = 3$, so split into three regions. $x < -1$: $(3-x) - (-x - 1) = 4 \ge -2$, always true, contributing $(-\infty, -1)$. $-1 \le x \le 3$: $(3-x) - (x+1) = 2 - 2x \ge -2$, giving $x \le 2$, contributing $[-1, 2]$. $x > 3$: $(x - 3) - (x+1) = -4 \ge -2$ is false, contributing nothing. Combining: $(-\infty, 2]$ — the stated $(-\infty, 2)$ wrongly excludes the endpoint $x = 2$, which comes from a non-strict ( $\ge$ ) condition and does satisfy the inequality.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 2$: $|2-3| - |2+1| = 1 - 3 = -2$, and is -2 $\ge$ -2? Yes — so $x = 2$ must be included, disproving the open interval.

**C) The inequality ${3 < x^{2} + 2x - 1 < 11}$ has solution set $(-1 - \sqrt{13}, -1 - \sqrt{5}) \cup (-1 + \sqrt{5}, -1 + \sqrt{13})$.**  (true)

**Left part**

$x^{2} + 2x - 1 > 3$

$x^{2} + 2x - 4 > 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = -1 \pm \sqrt{5}$, and since the parabola opens upward, the solution is $x < -1 - \sqrt{5}$ or $x > -1 + \sqrt{5}$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} + 2x - 1 < 11$

$x^{2} + 2x - 12 < 0$. The roots are $x = -1 \pm \sqrt{13}$, giving $-1 - \sqrt{13} < x < -1 + \sqrt{13}$. 

**Intersection**

$(-1 - \sqrt{13}, -1 - \sqrt{5}) \cup (-1 + \sqrt{5}, -1 + \sqrt{13})$ — matches exactly.

**D) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{x + 3} + \sqrt{x + 8} \le 5$ is $[-3, 1]$.**  (true)

**Domain**

$x + 3 \ge 0$ and $x + 8 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -3$. Isolate one radical: $\sqrt{x+3} \le 5 - \sqrt{x+8}$. Square: $x+3 \le 25 - 10\sqrt{x+8} + (x+8)$

${10\sqrt{x+8} \le 30}$

$\sqrt{x+8} \le 3$

$x \le 1$.

**Restrict to case**

Combined with $x \ge -3$: $[-3, 1]$; checking $x = 1$ gives $\sqrt{4} + \sqrt{9} = 2 + 3 = 5$, confirming equality at the boundary.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 25
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The solution set of the inequality $\bigl|\, |x + 3| - 5\bigr| < 4$ is $(-12, -4) \cup (-2, 6)$.
The inequality ${0 < x^{2} + 2x + 1 \le 9}$ has solution set $[-4, 2]$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{3x + 10} - \sqrt{x + 2} > 2$ is $x \ge -2$.
The solution set of the inequality $|5x + 2| \ge |2x - 9|$ is $x \le \frac{-11}{3}$ or $x \ge 1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The solution set of the inequality $\bigl|\, |x + 3| - 5\bigr| < 4$ is $(-12, -4) \cup (-2, 6)$.**  (true)

**First inequality**

$-4 < |x+3| - 5 < 4$, so ${1 < |x+3| < 9}$. Left part, $|x+3| > 1$, excludes $-4 \le x \le -2$ (keeping $x > -2$ or $x < -4$). Right part, $|x+3| < 9$, restricts to $-12 < x < 6$. Combining gives $(-12, -4) \cup (-2, 6)$.

**B) The inequality ${0 < x^{2} + 2x + 1 \le 9}$ has solution set $[-4, 2]$.**  (false)

**Left part**

$x^{2} + 2x + 1 > 0$

$(x+1)^{2} > 0$, true for every x except $x = -1$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} + 2x + 1 \le 9$

$x^{2} + 2x - 8 \le 0$

$(x+4)(x - 2) \le 0$

$-4 \le x \le 2$. 

**Intersection**

$[-4, 2]$ with $x = -1$ removed

$[-4, -1) \cup (-1, 2]$ — the stated $[-4, 2]$ wrongly includes $x = -1$.

**Common trap:** A perfect square being "strictly greater than 0" always excludes exactly the one point where it equals 0 — it’s easy to overlook this single gap when the rest of the interval looks continuous.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = -1$ directly: 1 - 2 + 1 = 0, and is 0 > 0? No — so $x = -1$ must be excluded, even though it sits inside $[-4, 2]$.

**C) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{3x + 10} - \sqrt{x + 2} > 2$ is $x \ge -2$.**  (false)

**Domain**

${3x + 10 \ge 0}$ and $x + 2 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -2$. Rewrite as $\sqrt{3x+10} > 2 + \sqrt{x+2}$. Squaring (right side $\ge$ 2 > 0): ${3x + 10 > 4 + 4\sqrt{x+2} + (x+2)}$

${2x + 4 > 4\sqrt{x+2}}$

$x + 2 > 2\sqrt{x+2}$. Let $u = \sqrt{x+2} \ge 0$ (so $x+2 = u^{2}$): the condition becomes $u^{2} > 2u$

$u(u - 2) > 0$

$u > 2$ (since $u \ge 0$). So $\sqrt{x+2} > 2$

$x + 2 > 4$

$x > 2$. The true solution is $x > 2$ — the domain alone $(x \ge -2)$ is nowhere near sufficient, since e.g. $x = 0$ satisfies the domain but fails the original inequality.

**Common trap:** The domain of a radical expression only guarantees the square roots are defined — after that, the inequality itself still needs to be solved, and that can carve away almost all of the domain.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 0$ (in the domain, far from the true cutoff $x = 2$): $\sqrt{10} - \sqrt{2} \approx 3.162 - 1.414 = 1.748$, which is not > 2 — disproving the domain-only claim.

**D) The solution set of the inequality $|5x + 2| \ge |2x - 9|$ is $x \le \frac{-11}{3}$ or $x \ge 1$.**  (true)

Since both sides are non-negative, squaring preserves the inequality: $(5x+2)^{2} \ge (2x - 9)^{2}$. Expanding: ${25x^{2} + 20x + 4 \ge 4x^{2} - 36x + 81}$

${21x^{2} + 56x - 77 \ge 0}$. Dividing by 7: ${3x^{2} + 8x - 11 \ge 0}$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = 1$ and $x = -$$\dfrac{11}{3}$. Since the parabola opens upward, it is non-negative outside (and at) its roots: $x \le -$$\dfrac{11}{3}$ or $x \ge 1$.

tasks.title: Compound & Special Inequalities — 26
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inequality $-2 \le x^{2} - 4x - 1 < 7$ has solution set $(2 - 2\sqrt{3}, 2 - \sqrt{3}] \cup [2 + \sqrt{3}, 2 + 2\sqrt{3})$.
The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{2x + 3} < \sqrt{5x + 4} - 1$ is $x > \dfrac{4 - 2\sqrt{31}}{9}$.
The solution set of the inequality $|x^{2} + x - 5| > 7$ is $x < -4$ or $x > 3$.
The inequality $-7 \le x^{2} - 2x - 6 < 3$ has solution set $(1 - \sqrt{10}, 1 + \sqrt{10})$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The inequality $-2 \le x^{2} - 4x - 1 < 7$ has solution set $(2 - 2\sqrt{3}, 2 - \sqrt{3}] \cup [2 + \sqrt{3}, 2 + 2\sqrt{3})$.**  (true)

**Left part**

$x^{2} - 4x - 1 \ge -2$

$x^{2} - 4x + 1 \ge 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = 2 \pm \sqrt{3}$, and since the parabola opens upward, the solution is $x \le 2 - \sqrt{3}$ or $x \ge 2 + \sqrt{3}$. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} - 4x - 1 < 7$

$x^{2} - 4x - 8 < 0$. The roots are $x = 2 \pm 2\sqrt{3}$, giving ${2 - 2\sqrt{3} < x < 2 + 2\sqrt{3}}$. 

**Intersection**

$(2 - 2\sqrt{3}, 2 - \sqrt{3}] \cup [2 + \sqrt{3}, 2 + 2\sqrt{3})$ — matches exactly.

**B) The solution set of the inequality $\sqrt{2x + 3} < \sqrt{5x + 4} - 1$ is $x > \dfrac{4 - 2\sqrt{31}}{9}$.**  (false)

**Domain**

${2x + 3 \ge 0}$ and ${5x + 4 \ge 0}$, so $x \ge -0.6$. Rewrite as $\sqrt{5x+4} > 1 + \sqrt{2x+3}$. Squaring (right side $\ge$ 0): ${5x + 4 > 1 + 2\sqrt{2x+3} + (2x+3)}$

${3x > 2\sqrt{2x+3}}$. The left side must be $\ge$ 0, forcing $x \ge 0$. Squaring again: ${9x^{2} > 4(2x+3)}$

${9x^{2} - 8x - 12 > 0}$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are x = $\dfrac{4 ± 2√31}{9}$. Since the parabola opens upward, it is positive outside the roots; combined with $x \ge 0$, only the larger root matters (since $\dfrac{4−2√31}{9}$ ≈ -0.79 is negative), giving $x >$ $\dfrac{4+2√31}{9}$ ≈ 1.68 — not the smaller root stated here.

**Quick check:** $\dfrac{4+2√31}{9}$ ≈ 1.68 and $\dfrac{4−2√31}{9}$ ≈ -0.79; since x must already be $\ge$ 0, only the larger root can be the true boundary.

**C) The solution set of the inequality $|x^{2} + x - 5| > 7$ is $x < -4$ or $x > 3$.**  (true)

Let y = $x^{2} + x - 5$. The inequality $|y| > 7$ splits into y > 7 or y < -7. Branch y > 7: $x^{2} + x - 12 > 0$

$(x+4)(x - 3) > 0$

$x < -4$ or $x > 3$. Branch y < -7: $x^{2} + x + 2 < 0$. The discriminant is 1 - 8 = -7, which is negative, and since the leading coefficient is positive, $x^{2} + x + 2$ is always positive — this branch has no real solutions at all. Only the first branch contributes: $x < -4$ or $x > 3$.

**D) The inequality $-7 \le x^{2} - 2x - 6 < 3$ has solution set $(1 - \sqrt{10}, 1 + \sqrt{10})$.**  (true)

**Left part**

$x^{2} - 2x - 6 \ge -7$

$x^{2} - 2x + 1 \ge 0$

$(x - 1)^{2} \ge 0$, which is true for every real x. 

**Right part**

$x^{2} - 2x - 6 < 3$

$x^{2} - 2x - 9 < 0$.

By the quadratic formula, the roots are $x = 1 \pm \sqrt{10}$, giving ${1 - \sqrt{10} < x < 1 + \sqrt{10}}$.

Since the left condition never restricts anything, the full solution is exactly $(1 - \sqrt{10}, 1 + \sqrt{10})$.

tasks.title: Loyalty Points Discount
tasks.context: A wireless carrier's monthly bill is $400, but each loyalty point redeemed lowers the bill by $0.50. Let x represent the number of points redeemed. A customer wants their bill to be $250 or less.
statements: Redeeming 300 points brings the bill to exactly $250.
Redeeming 250 points brings the bill to $250 or less.
Redeeming 350 points brings the bill below $250.
The minimum number of points that must be redeemed is 300.
Solving the inequality ${400 - 0.5x \le 250}$ by dividing both sides by -0.5 gives $x \le 300$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Redeeming 300 points brings the bill to exactly $250.**  (true)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${400 - 0.5x \le 250}$ gives $-0.5x \le -150$.

**Solve**

Dividing both sides by -0.5 (a negative number) flips the inequality, giving $x \ge 300$. At $x = 300$, the bill is exactly at the target.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 300$: 400 - 0.5(300) = 400 - 150 = 250, exactly at the $250 target.

**B) Redeeming 250 points brings the bill to $250 or less.**  (false)

At $x = 250$, the bill is 400 - 0.5(250) = 275, which is more than $250, so this does not meet the target.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 250$: 400 - 125 = 275, and 275 is not $\le$ 250.

**C) Redeeming 350 points brings the bill below $250.**  (true)

At $x = 350$, the bill is 400 - 0.5(350) = 225, which is below $250.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 350$: 400 - 175 = 225 < 250.

**D) The minimum number of points that must be redeemed is 300.**  (true)

**Conclusion**

This restates the solved inequality $x \ge 300$, so the minimum number of points needed is indeed 300.

**E) Solving the inequality ${400 - 0.5x \le 250}$ by dividing both sides by -0.5 gives $x \le 300$.**  (false)

**Solve**

Isolating x from $-0.5x \le -150$ requires dividing by -0.5, a negative number, which flips the inequality direction. The correct result is $x \ge 300$, not $x \le 300$.

**Quick check:** plug in a value that satisfies $x \ge 300$, like $x = 310$: 400 - 0.5(310) = 245 $\le$ 250 ✓, but a value that satisfies the wrongly stated $x \le 300$, like $x = 100$: 400 - 0.5(100) = 350, which is not $\le$ 250 — disproving $x \le 300$.
tasks.solution_overview: A wireless carrier's monthly bill is $400, but each loyalty point redeemed lowers the bill by $0.50. Let x represent the number of points redeemed. A customer wants their bill to be $250 or less.

tasks.title: Store Membership Savings
tasks.context: A store membership costs $40 per year. Members get a flat 20% discount on all purchases. Let s represent the total sticker price (non-member price) of a shopper's purchases over a year. The shopper wants to know when membership actually saves money — that is, when (membership fee + discounted total) is less than paying the sticker price with no membership.
statements: If a shopper spends $250 (sticker price) in a year, membership saves them money.
If a shopper spends $150, membership saves them money.
At exactly $200 spent, membership costs the same as not joining.
The minimum amount a shopper must spend for membership to be worthwhile is more than $200.
The inequality that models “membership saves money” is correctly written as ${40 + 0.8s > s}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If a shopper spends $250 (sticker price) in a year, membership saves them money.**  (true)

“Saves money” means ${40 + 0.8s < s}$. With $s = 250$: 40 + 0.8(250) = 240, which is less than the $250 sticker price without membership.

**Quick check:** plug in $s = 250$: 40 + 200 = 240 < 250.

**B) If a shopper spends $150, membership saves them money.**  (false)

With $s = 150$: 40 + 0.8(150) = 160, which is more than the $150 sticker price — membership does not pay off yet at this spending level.

**Quick check:** plug in $s = 150$: 40 + 120 = 160, and 160 > 150.

**C) At exactly $200 spent, membership costs the same as not joining.**  (true)

With $s = 200$: 40 + 0.8(200) = 200, exactly equal to the $200 sticker price — the break-even point.

**Quick check:** plug in $s = 200$: 40 + 160 = 200 = 200.

**D) The minimum amount a shopper must spend for membership to be worthwhile is more than $200.**  (true)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${40 + 0.8s < s}$ gives ${40 < 0.2s}$, so $s > 200$. This restates the solved inequality.

**E) The inequality that models “membership saves money” is correctly written as ${40 + 0.8s > s}$.**  (false)

“Membership saves money” means the membership total is less than the non-member sticker price, so the correct inequality uses “<”, not “>”.

The shopper wants to know when membership actually saves money — that is, when (membership fee + discounted total) is less than paying the sticker price with no membership.

tasks.title: Greenhouse Temperature Safety
tasks.context: A greenhouse's automated cooling system monitors temperature in Fahrenheit $(F)$, converted to Celsius using $C = \frac{5}{9}(F - 32)$. For plant safety, the Celsius reading must stay at or below 30°C.
statements: A reading of 86°F keeps the greenhouse at exactly 30°C.
A reading of 90°F is within the safe range.
A reading of 80°F is within the safe range.
The maximum safe Fahrenheit reading is 86°F.
Since the safety limit is 30°C, the equivalent Fahrenheit safety limit is also 30°F.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A reading of 86°F keeps the greenhouse at exactly 30°C.**  (true)

($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(86 - 32) = ($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(54) = 30, exactly at the limit.

**Quick check:** plug in $F = 86$: ($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(54) = 30.

**B) A reading of 90°F is within the safe range.**  (false)

($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(90 - 32) = ($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(58) ≈ 32.2°C, which is above the 30°C limit.

**Quick check:** plug in $F = 90$: ($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(58) ≈ 32.2 > 30.

**C) A reading of 80°F is within the safe range.**  (true)

($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(80 - 32) = ($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(48) ≈ 26.7°C, which is within the limit.

**Quick check:** plug in $F = 80$: ($\dfrac{5}{9}$)(48) ≈ 26.7 < 30.

**D) The maximum safe Fahrenheit reading is 86°F.**  (true)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ($\dfrac{5}{9}$)$(F - 32) \le 30$ gives $F - 32 \le 54$, so $F \le 86$. This matches the solved inequality.

**E) Since the safety limit is 30°C, the equivalent Fahrenheit safety limit is also 30°F.**  (false)

A 30°C limit does not correspond to a 30°F limit — the two scales are not interchangeable number-for-number. Converting properly through the inequality shows the equivalent Fahrenheit limit is 86°F, not 30°F.
tasks.solution_overview: A greenhouse's automated cooling system monitors temperature in Fahrenheit $(F)$, converted to Celsius using $C = \frac{5}{9}(F - 32)$. For plant safety, the Celsius reading must stay at or below 30°C.

tasks.title: Paying Off a Loan
tasks.context: Jordan borrowed $2,400 with no interest. He already made an initial payment of $300, and now plans to pay $150 per month. Let m represent the number of additional monthly payments he makes. He wants to know when the remaining balance reaches $0 or less (fully paid off).
statements: After 14 additional monthly payments, the loan is fully paid off.
After 13 additional monthly payments, the loan is fully paid off.
After 15 additional monthly payments, Jordan will have overpaid (the balance is negative).
The minimum number of additional months needed is 14.
Solving the inequality 2100 - 150m $\le$ 0 by dividing both sides by -150 gives m $\le$ 14.
tactical_explanations:
**A) After 14 additional monthly payments, the loan is fully paid off.**  (true)

Remaining balance after the initial payment: 2400 - 300 = 2100. Solving 2100 - 150m $\le$ 0 gives -150m $\le$ -2100.

**Solve**

Dividing both sides by -150 flips the inequality, giving m $\ge$ 14. At m = 14, the balance reaches exactly $0.

**Quick check:** plug in m = 14: 2100 - 150(14) = 2100 - 2100 = 0.

**B) After 13 additional monthly payments, the loan is fully paid off.**  (false)

At m = 13: 2100 - 150(13) = 150, so Jordan still owes $150 — not yet paid off.

**Quick check:** plug in m = 13: 2100 - 1950 = 150 $\ne$ 0.

**C) After 15 additional monthly payments, Jordan will have overpaid (the balance is negative).**  (true)

At m = 15: 2100 - 150(15) = -150, a negative balance, meaning Jordan overpaid by $150.

**Quick check:** plug in m = 15: 2100 - 2250 = -150 < 0.

**D) The minimum number of additional months needed is 14.**  (true)

**Conclusion**

This restates the solved inequality m $\ge$ 14.

**E) Solving the inequality 2100 - 150m $\le$ 0 by dividing both sides by -150 gives m $\le$ 14.**  (false)

**Solve**

Isolating m from -150m $\le$ -2100 requires dividing by -150, a negative number, which flips the inequality direction. The correct result is m $\ge$ 14, not m $\le$ 14.

**Quick check:** plug in m = 20 (satisfies the correct m $\ge$ 14): 2100 - 150(20) = -900 $\le$ 0 ✓; but m = 20 does not satisfy the wrongly stated m $\le$ 14, showing that statement is inconsistent with a value that clearly should work.

tasks.title: Restaurant Service Charge
tasks.context: A restaurant adds a 20% service charge to the bill. Let B represent the pre-charge bill amount. A customer wants the total (bill plus service charge) to stay under $300.
statements: A pre-charge bill of $200 results in a total under $300.
A pre-charge bill of $260 results in a total under $300.
A pre-charge bill of exactly $250 results in a total under $300.
The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as 1.2B < 300.
Solving 1.2B < 300 by dividing both sides by 1.2 keeps the inequality direction the same (since 1.2 is positive), giving B < 250.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A pre-charge bill of $200 results in a total under $300.**  (true)

1.2(200) = 240, which is under $300.

**Quick check:** plug in B = 200: 1.2(200) = 240 < 300.

**B) A pre-charge bill of $260 results in a total under $300.**  (false)

1.2(260) = 312, which is over $300.

**Quick check:** plug in B = 260: 1.2(260) = 312 > 300.

**C) A pre-charge bill of exactly $250 results in a total under $300.**  (false)

1.2(250) = 300 exactly, and the target requires the total to be strictly under $300, so this boundary value does not satisfy the condition.

**Quick check:** plug in B = 250: 1.2(250) = 300, and 300 is not strictly less than 300.

**D) The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as 1.2B < 300.**  (true)

The bill plus 20% of the bill equals B + 0.2B = 1.2B, and this total must be less than $300, giving 1.2B < 300.

**E) Solving 1.2B < 300 by dividing both sides by 1.2 keeps the inequality direction the same (since 1.2 is positive), giving B < 250.**  (true)

Since 1.2 is a positive number, dividing both sides of 1.2B < 300 by 1.2 does not flip the inequality direction, giving B < 250 correctly. This contrasts with Questions 4 and 7, where the coefficient being isolated was negative and the inequality direction did flip.

tasks.title: Basketball Scoring Average
tasks.context: A basketball player wants a season average of at least 20 points per game across her first 5 games. Her scores in the first 4 games were 18, 22, 19, and 17 points. Let x represent her score in the 5th game.
statements: Scoring 24 points in the 5th game meets the average goal exactly.
Scoring 23 points in the 5th game meets the average goal.
The minimum score she needs in the 5th game is 20 points.
Scoring 30 points in the 5th game would raise her average above 20.
Clearing the fraction in $\dfrac{18+22+19+17+x}{5} \ge 20$ gives ${76 + x \ge 100}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Scoring 24 points in the 5th game meets the average goal exactly.**  (true)

$\dfrac{18+22+19+17+x}{5}$ $\ge$ 20

${76+x \ge 100}$

$x \ge 24$. At $x = 24$, the average is exactly 20.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 24$: $\dfrac{76+24}{5}$ = $\dfrac{100}{5}$ = 20.

**B) Scoring 23 points in the 5th game meets the average goal.**  (false)

With $x = 23$: $\dfrac{76+23}{5}$ = $\dfrac{99}{5}$ = 19.8, which is below the 20-point target.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 23$: total = 99, average = 19.8 < 20.

**C) The minimum score she needs in the 5th game is 20 points.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. the inequality gives $x \ge 24$, meaning the 5th game score itself must be at least 24 — not 20. The number 20 is the target average, not the target score for this specific game.

**Common trap:** This is the same trap that shows up in every average-threshold problem: the number stated in the problem $(20, the$ target average) is easy to confuse with the number actually required in the inequality's solution $(24, the$ needed score). Whenever earlier results sit below the target average, the score still needed will always be higher than the target itself — solving the inequality is the only reliable way to find it.

**D) Scoring 30 points in the 5th game would raise her average above 20.**  (true)

With $x = 30$: $\dfrac{76+30}{5}$ = $\dfrac{106}{5}$ = 21.2, which is above 20.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 30$: total = 106, average = 21.2 > 20.

**E) Clearing the fraction in $\dfrac{18+22+19+17+x}{5} \ge 20$ gives ${76 + x \ge 100}$.**  (true)

Multiplying both sides of $\dfrac{76+x}{5}$ $\ge$ 20 by 5 gives ${76+x \ge 100}$, which correctly clears the denominator.

tasks.title: Manufacturing Quality Control
tasks.context: A cereal factory must pack a batch of 6 boxes with an average weight of at least 350 grams to meet regulations. The weights of the first 5 boxes were ${340g}$, ${355g}$, ${345g}$, ${360g}$, and ${338g}$. Let x represent the weight of the 6th box.
statements: A 6th box weighing ${362g}$ meets the regulation exactly.
A 6th box weighing ${360g}$ meets the regulation.
The minimum weight needed for the 6th box is ${350g}$.
A 6th box weighing ${400g}$ results in a batch average above ${350g}$.
Multiplying both sides of $\dfrac{1738+x}{6} \ge 350$ by 6 gives ${1738 + x \ge 2100}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A 6th box weighing ${362g}$ meets the regulation exactly.**  (true)

First 5 weights sum to ${340+355+345+360+338 = 1738g}$. $\dfrac{1738+x}{6}$ $\ge$ 350

${1738+x \ge 2100}$

$x \ge 362$. At $x = 362$, the average is exactly ${350g}$.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 362$: $\dfrac{1738+362}{6}$ = $\dfrac{2100}{6}$ = 350.

**B) A 6th box weighing ${360g}$ meets the regulation.**  (false)

With $x = 360$: $\dfrac{1738+360}{6}$ = $\dfrac{2098}{6}$ ≈ 349.67, which is below the ${350g}$ requirement.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 360$: total = 2098, average ≈ 349.67 < 350.

**C) The minimum weight needed for the 6th box is ${350g}$.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. the inequality gives $x \ge 362$, meaning the 6th box itself must weigh at least ${362g}$ — not ${350g}$. The number 350 is the target batch average, not the target weight for this specific box.

**Common trap:** Same trap as in the basketball scoring problem, in a different dressing: the target average $(350g)$ and the actual weight needed for the last item $(362g)$ are two different numbers. Because the first 5 boxes averaged below ${350g}$, the 6th box has to compensate by weighing more than the target average itself.

**D) A 6th box weighing ${400g}$ results in a batch average above ${350g}$.**  (true)

With $x = 400$: $\dfrac{1738+400}{6}$ = $\dfrac{2138}{6}$ ≈ 356.33, which is above 350.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 400$: total = 2138, average ≈ 356.33 > 350.

**E) Multiplying both sides of $\dfrac{1738+x}{6} \ge 350$ by 6 gives ${1738 + x \ge 2100}$.**  (true)

Multiplying both sides of $\dfrac{1738+x}{6}$ $\ge$ 350 by 6 correctly clears the denominator, giving ${1738+x \ge 2100}$.

tasks.title: Rideshare Surge Pricing
tasks.context: A rideshare app normally charges a $2.50 base fee plus $1.75 per mile. During surge pricing, the entire fare (base fee plus mileage charge) is multiplied by 1.5. Let m represent the number of miles. A rider wants a surge-priced trip to cost no more than $30.
statements: A 10-mile trip during surge pricing costs exactly $30.
A 12-mile trip during surge pricing stays within the $30 limit.
The maximum number of miles that keeps a surge-priced trip at or under $30 is 10 miles.
Distributing the 1.5 multiplier across the parentheses first gives 3.75 + 2.625m $\le$ 30.
Multiplying only the $2.50 base fee by 1.5 (and leaving the $1.75 per-mile rate unmultiplied) also produces the correct maximum number of miles.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A 10-mile trip during surge pricing costs exactly $30.**  (true)

The full surge fare is 1.5(2.5 + 1.75m). Distributing: 3.75 + 2.625m $\le$ 30

2.625m $\le$ 26.25

m $\le$ 10. At m = 10, the fare is exactly $30.

**Quick check:** plug in m = 10: 1.5 $\times$ (2.5 + 17.5) = 1.5 $\times$ 20 = 30.

**B) A 12-mile trip during surge pricing stays within the $30 limit.**  (false)

At m = 12: 1.5 $\times$ (2.5 + 21) = 1.5 $\times$ 23.5 = 35.25, which is over $30.

**Quick check:** plug in m = 12: 1.5 $\times$ 23.5 = 35.25 > 30.

**C) The maximum number of miles that keeps a surge-priced trip at or under $30 is 10 miles.**  (true)

**Conclusion**

This restates the solved inequality m $\le$ 10.

**D) Distributing the 1.5 multiplier across the parentheses first gives 3.75 + 2.625m $\le$ 30.**  (true)

1.5(2.5 + 1.75m) = 1.5(2.5) + 1.5(1.75m) = 3.75 + 2.625m, correctly distributing the surge multiplier across both terms.

**E) Multiplying only the $2.50 base fee by 1.5 (and leaving the $1.75 per-mile rate unmultiplied) also produces the correct maximum number of miles.**  (false)

Multiplying only the base fee gives 3.75 + 1.75m $\le$ 30

1.75m $\le$ 26.25

m $\le$ 15, which does not match the correct answer of m $\le$ 10.

**Quick check:** plug in m = 15 (the wrong cutoff) into the correct fare formula: 1.5 $\times$ (2.5 + 1.75 $\times$ 15) = 1.5 $\times$ 28.75 = 43.125, which is far over $30 — disproving m $\le$ 15 as a valid cutoff.
tasks.solution_overview: A rideshare app normally charges a $2.50 base fee plus $1.75 per mile. During surge pricing, the entire fare (base fee plus mileage charge) is multiplied by 1.5. Let m represent the number of miles. A rider wants a surge-priced trip to cost no more than $30.

tasks.title: Discount and Coupon Order
tasks.context: A store applies a 25% discount to an item's original price, then subtracts an additional flat $15 coupon. Let p represent the original price. The final price is ${0.75p - 15}$. A customer wants the final price to be $60 or less.
statements: An original price of $100 results in a final price of exactly $60.
An original price of $120 keeps the final price at or under $60.
The maximum original price that keeps the final price at or under $60 is $100.
Applying the $15 coupon before the 25% discount instead — that is, ${0.75(p - 15) \le 60}$ — gives the same maximum original price of $100.
The inequality correctly modeling “discount first, then flat coupon” is ${0.75p - 15 \le 60}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) An original price of $100 results in a final price of exactly $60.**  (true)

${0.75p - 15 \le 60}$

${0.75p \le 75}$

$p \le 100$. At $p = 100$, the final price is exactly $60.

**Quick check:** plug in $p = 100$: 0.75(100) - 15 = 75 - 15 = 60.

**B) An original price of $120 keeps the final price at or under $60.**  (false)

At $p = 120$: 0.75(120) - 15 = 90 - 15 = 75, which is over $60.

**Quick check:** plug in $p = 120$: 90 - 15 = 75 > 60.

**C) The maximum original price that keeps the final price at or under $60 is $100.**  (true)

**Conclusion**

This restates the solved inequality $p \le 100$.

**D) Applying the $15 coupon before the 25% discount instead — that is, ${0.75(p - 15) \le 60}$ — gives the same maximum original price of $100.**  (false)

**Order of operations**

Applying the coupon first: ${0.75(p - 15) \le 60}$

$p - 15 \le 80$

$p \le 95$. This maximum ($95) is different from the maximum when the discount is applied first ($100), so the two orders do not give the same result.

**Common trap:** Percentage discounts and flat-amount coupons don't commute — applying them in a different order changes the final price, because the percentage is taken off a different base amount each time. Always apply the operations in the exact order the problem describes, rather than assuming the order doesn't matter.

**Quick check:** compare directly: discount-then-coupon at $p = 100$ gives 0.75(100)-15=60; coupon-then-discount at the same $p = 100$ gives 0.75(100-15)=63.75 — different final prices for the same original price, confirming order matters.

**E) The inequality correctly modeling “discount first, then flat coupon” is ${0.75p - 15 \le 60}$.**  (true)

“Discount first” means the 25% reduction applies to the original price p, giving ${0.75p}$, and then the flat $15 coupon is subtracted after, giving ${0.75p - 15 \le 60}$.
tasks.solution_overview: A store applies a 25% discount to an item's original price, then subtracts an additional flat $15 coupon. Let p represent the original price. The final price is ${0.75p - 15}$. A customer wants the final price to be $60 or less.

tasks.title: Average Cycling Speed
tasks.context: A cyclist wants her average speed to be at least 15 mph over a 2-hour trip, where she rides at a constant speed during each 1-hour segment. In the first hour, she rode at 12 mph. Let x represent her speed, in mph, during the second hour.
statements: Riding at 18 mph in the second hour meets the average goal exactly.
Riding at 17 mph in the second hour meets the average goal.
The minimum speed she needs in the second hour is 15 mph.
Riding at 20 mph in the second hour results in an average above 15 mph.
The inequality $\dfrac{12+x}{2} \ge 15$ correctly models the average-speed requirement.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Riding at 18 mph in the second hour meets the average goal exactly.**  (true)

$\dfrac{12+x}{2}$ $\ge$ 15

${12+x \ge 30}$

$x \ge 18$. At $x = 18$, the average speed is exactly 15 mph.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 18$: $\dfrac{12+18}{2}$ = $\dfrac{30}{2}$ = 15.

**B) Riding at 17 mph in the second hour meets the average goal.**  (false)

With $x = 17$: $\dfrac{12+17}{2}$ = $\dfrac{29}{2}$ = 14.5, which is below the 15 mph target.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 17$: total = 29, average = 14.5 < 15.

**C) The minimum speed she needs in the second hour is 15 mph.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. the inequality gives $x \ge 18$, meaning the second-hour speed itself must be at least 18 mph — not 15 mph. The number 15 is the target average speed, not the target speed for this specific hour.

**Common trap:** The number 15 is the target average speed, not the minimum speed required in the second hour when the first segment falls below that goal.

**D) Riding at 20 mph in the second hour results in an average above 15 mph.**  (true)

With $x = 20$: $\dfrac{12+20}{2}$ = $\dfrac{32}{2}$ = 16, which is above 15.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 20$: total = 32, average = 16 > 15.

**E) The inequality $\dfrac{12+x}{2} \ge 15$ correctly models the average-speed requirement.**  (true)

**Setup**

Average speed equals total distance divided by total time. The first hour covers 12 miles and the second covers x miles, so the average is $\dfrac{12+x}{2}$.

**Inequality**

Requiring at least 15 mph over 2 hours gives $\dfrac{12+x}{2}$ $\ge$ 15.
tasks.solution_overview: A cyclist wants her average speed to be at least 15 mph over a 2-hour trip, where she rides at a constant speed during each 1-hour segment. In the first hour, she rode at 12 mph. Let x represent her speed, in mph, during the second hour.

tasks.title: Wedding Catering Budget
tasks.context: A couple wants their catering cost to be at least $3,000 but no more than $4,500. Catering costs a $500 setup fee plus $75 per guest. Let g represent the number of guests (a whole number).
statements: 34 guests satisfies both budget requirements.
33 guests satisfies both budget requirements.
53 guests satisfies both budget requirements.
54 guests satisfies both budget requirements.
The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as ${3000 \le 500 + 75g \le 4500}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) 34 guests satisfies both budget requirements.**  (true)

**Evaluate**

500 + 75(34) = 500 + 2550 = 3050, which is between $3,000 and $4,500.

**Quick check:** plug in $g = 34$: 500 + 2550 = 3050, and 3000 $\le$ 3050 $\le$ 4500.

**B) 33 guests satisfies both budget requirements.**  (false)

**Evaluate**

500 + 75(33) = 500 + 2475 = 2975, which is below the $3,000 minimum.

**Quick check:** plug in $g = 33$: 500 + 2475 = 2975 < 3000.

**C) 53 guests satisfies both budget requirements.**  (true)

**Evaluate**

500 + 75(53) = 500 + 3975 = 4475, which is at or under the $4,500 maximum.

**Quick check:** plug in $g = 53$: 500 + 3975 = 4475 $\le$ 4500.

**D) 54 guests satisfies both budget requirements.**  (false)

**Evaluate**

500 + 75(54) = 500 + 4050 = 4550, which is over the $4,500 maximum.

**Quick check:** plug in $g = 54$: 500 + 4050 = 4550 > 4500.

**E) The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as ${3000 \le 500 + 75g \le 4500}$.**  (true)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. each half separately: ${500+75g \ge 3000}$ gives $g \ge 33.33$..., and ${500+75g \le 4500}$ gives $g \le 53.33$ Combined: 33.33... $\le g \le 53.33$

**Common trap:** Because g must be a whole number of guests, the two boundaries round in opposite directions: the lower bound (33.33...) rounds UP to 34 to guarantee spending at least $3,000, while the upper bound (53.33...) rounds DOWN to 53 to avoid exceeding $4,500. A single compound inequality can require rounding in both directions at once — always check which direction each boundary needs before rounding.
tasks.solution_overview: A couple wants their catering cost to be at least $3,000 but no more than $4,500. Catering costs a $500 setup fee plus $75 per guest. Let g represent the number of guests (a whole number).

tasks.title: Bulk Soil Purchase
tasks.context: A gardener needs at least 47 kg of soil for a project. Soil is sold only in 5 kg bags. Let n represent the number of bags purchased (a whole number).
statements: Buying 9 bags provides enough soil.
Buying 10 bags provides enough soil.
The minimum number of whole bags needed is 9.
Buying 10 bags results in 3 kg of leftover soil beyond what's needed.
Solving ${5n \ge 47}$ gives $n \ge 9.4$, and since n must be a whole number, the correct minimum is found by rounding up to 10, not down to 9.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Buying 9 bags provides enough soil.**  (false)

5(9) = 45 kg, which is less than the 47 kg needed.

**Quick check:** plug in $n = 9$: 5(9) = 45 < 47.

**B) Buying 10 bags provides enough soil.**  (true)

5(10) = 50 kg, which meets the 47 kg requirement.

**Quick check:** plug in $n = 10$: 5(10) = 50 $\ge$ 47.

**C) The minimum number of whole bags needed is 9.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${5n \ge 47}$ gives $n \ge 9.4$. Since 9 bags only provide 45 kg (not enough), 9 is not a valid minimum — 10 bags are required.

**D) Buying 10 bags results in 3 kg of leftover soil beyond what's needed.**  (true)

5(10) - 47 = 50 - 47 = 3 kg of leftover soil.

**E) Solving ${5n \ge 47}$ gives $n \ge 9.4$, and since n must be a whole number, the correct minimum is found by rounding up to 10, not down to 9.**  (true)

This correctly describes both the algebraic solution $(n \ge 9.4)$ and the real-world rounding rule (round up to 10, since 9 bags fall short).
tasks.solution_overview: A gardener needs at least 47 kg of soil for a project. Soil is sold only in 5 kg bags. Let n represent the number of bags purchased (a whole number).

tasks.title: Weighted Course Grade
tasks.context: A student's course grade is weighted: homework counts for 20%, the midterm counts for 30%, and the final exam counts for 50%. She scored 85 on homework and 78 on the midterm. She wants an overall grade of at least 80. Let x represent her final exam score.
statements: Scoring 80 on the final exam meets her grade goal.
Scoring 79 on the final exam meets her grade goal.
The minimum final exam score she needs is 80.
Scoring 90 on the final exam results in an overall grade above 85.
This is a weighted average, so the setup differs from the simple averages in Questions 9, 10, and 13, since each component contributes a different proportion to the total rather than equal parts.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Scoring 80 on the final exam meets her grade goal.**  (true)

${0.2(85) + 0.3(78) + 0.5x \ge 80}$

${17 + 23.4 + 0.5x \ge 80}$

${40.4 + 0.5x \ge 80}$

$x \ge 79.2$. At $x = 80$, the overall grade is 40.4+40=80.4, which meets the goal.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 80$: 17 + 23.4 + 0.5(80) = 17+23.4+40 = 80.4 $\ge$ 80.

**B) Scoring 79 on the final exam meets her grade goal.**  (false)

With $x = 79$: 17 + 23.4 + 0.5(79) = 17+23.4+39.5 = 79.9, which is below the 80 goal.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 79$: total = 79.9 < 80.

**C) The minimum final exam score she needs is 80.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. the inequality gives $x \ge 79.2$, meaning the final exam score itself must be at least 79.2 — not 80.

**D) Scoring 90 on the final exam results in an overall grade above 85.**  (true)

With $x = 90$: 17 + 23.4 + 0.5(90) = 17+23.4+45 = 85.4, which is above 85.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 90$: total = 85.4 > 85.

**E) This is a weighted average, so the setup differs from the simple averages in Questions 9, 10, and 13, since each component contributes a different proportion to the total rather than equal parts.**  (true)

In Questions 9, 10, and 13, every value contributed equally to the average (divide the sum by the count). Here, each component is multiplied by its own weight $(0.2, 0.3, 0.5)$ before being added, so the algebra involves an extra multiplication step per term.
tasks.solution_overview: A student's course grade is weighted: homework counts for 20%, the midterm counts for 30%, and the final exam counts for 50%. She scored 85 on homework and 78 on the midterm. She wants an overall grade of at least 80. Let x represent her final exam score.

tasks.title: Simple Interest Savings
tasks.context: Emma invests $2,000 in an account earning 4% simple annual interest, so the balance after t years is ${2000 + 80t}$. She wants the balance to exceed $2,600.
statements: After 7.5 years, the balance is exactly $2,600.
After 7 full years, the balance exceeds $2,600.
After 8 full years, the balance exceeds $2,600.
Since interest is credited once per full year, the minimum number of full years needed for the balance to exceed $2,600 is 8 years.
The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as ${2000 + 80t > 2600}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) After 7.5 years, the balance is exactly $2,600.**  (true)

2000 + 80(7.5) = 2000 + 600 = 2600, exactly at the boundary value.

**Quick check:** plug in $t = 7.5$: 2000 + 600 = 2600.

**B) After 7 full years, the balance exceeds $2,600.**  (false)

2000 + 80(7) = 2000 + 560 = 2560, which does not exceed $2,600.

**Quick check:** plug in $t = 7$: 2000 + 560 = 2560 < 2600.

**C) After 8 full years, the balance exceeds $2,600.**  (true)

2000 + 80(8) = 2000 + 640 = 2640, which exceeds $2,600.

**Quick check:** plug in $t = 8$: 2000 + 640 = 2640 > 2600.

**D) Since interest is credited once per full year, the minimum number of full years needed for the balance to exceed $2,600 is 8 years.**  (true)

Algebraically, $t > 7.5$ solves the inequality. But $t = 7.5$ itself does not satisfy the strict inequality (2600 is not > 2600), and years are only counted in whole numbers here, so the practical minimum is the next full year: 8.

**E) The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as ${2000 + 80t > 2600}$.**  (true)

“Exceed $2,600” means strictly greater than $2,600, so the correct inequality uses “>”: ${2000 + 80t > 2600}$.
tasks.solution_overview: Emma invests $2,000 in an account earning 4% simple annual interest, so the balance after t years is ${2000 + 80t}$. She wants the balance to exceed $2,600.

tasks.title: Sales Tax Budget
tasks.context: A shopper's state charges 8% sales tax on top of the listed price. She has $54 total to spend, including tax. Let p represent the pre-tax listed price of the items she buys.
statements: A pre-tax total of $50 keeps her within budget after tax.
A pre-tax total of $52 keeps her within budget after tax.
The maximum pre-tax amount she can spend is $50.
If the tax rate were 10% instead of 8%, the maximum pre-tax amount she could spend would be lower than $50.
The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as $p + 0.08 \le 54$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A pre-tax total of $50 keeps her within budget after tax.**  (true)

1.08(50) = 54, exactly at the budget limit.

**Quick check:** plug in $p = 50$: 1.08(50) = 54 $\le$ 54.

**B) A pre-tax total of $52 keeps her within budget after tax.**  (false)

1.08(52) = 56.16, which is over the $54 budget.

**Quick check:** plug in $p = 52$: 1.08(52) = 56.16 > 54.

**C) The maximum pre-tax amount she can spend is $50.**  (true)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${1.08p \le 54}$ gives $p \le 50$, matching the maximum pre-tax amount.

**D) If the tax rate were 10% instead of 8%, the maximum pre-tax amount she could spend would be lower than $50.**  (true)

With a 10% tax rate: ${1.10p \le 54}$

$p \le 49.09$..., which is indeed lower than $50.

**Quick check:** plug in the 10% version at $p = 50$: 1.10(50) = 55, which is over $54, confirming $50 no longer works at the higher rate.

**E) The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as $p + 0.08 \le 54$.**  (false)

A percentage must be multiplied by the value it applies to before being added — the tax owed is ${0.08p (8% of the}$ price), not a flat 0.08. The correct total is $p + 0.08p = 1.08p \le 54$, not $p + 0.08 \le 54$.
tasks.solution_overview: A shopper's state charges 8% sales tax on top of the listed price. She has $54 total to spend, including tax. Let p represent the pre-tax listed price of the items she buys.

tasks.title: Overtime Pay
tasks.context: An employee earns $18/hour for the first 40 hours worked in a week, and time-and-a-half ($27/hour) for each hour beyond 40. Let h represent total hours worked in a week $(h > 40)$. She wants her weekly pay to be at least $850.
statements: Working 45 hours results in pay of at least $850.
Working 44 hours results in pay of at least $850.
The minimum number of whole hours needed to earn at least $850 is 44.
Working 50 hours results in pay of more than $900.
Calculating pay for 45 hours as simply 18 $\times$ 45 (ignoring the higher overtime rate for hours beyond 40) gives the same total as the correct formula.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Working 45 hours results in pay of at least $850.**  (true)

Pay = ${18(40) + 27(h - 40) = 720 + 27h - 1080 = 27h - 360}$ for $h > 40$. At $h = 45$: 27(45)-360 = 1215-360 = 855, which is at least $850.

**Quick check:** plug in $h = 45$: 27(45) - 360 = 855 $\ge$ 850.

**B) Working 44 hours results in pay of at least $850.**  (false)

At $h = 44$: 27(44)-360 = 1188-360 = 828, which is below $850.

**Quick check:** plug in $h = 44$: 27(44) - 360 = 828 < 850.

**C) The minimum number of whole hours needed to earn at least $850 is 44.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${27h - 360 \ge 850}$ gives $h \ge 44.81$..., and since 44 hours only earns $828 (not enough), the minimum whole number of hours is actually 45, not 44.

**D) Working 50 hours results in pay of more than $900.**  (true)

At $h = 50$: 27(50)-360 = 1350-360 = 990, which is more than $900.

**Quick check:** plug in $h = 50$: 27(50) - 360 = 990 > 900.

**E) Calculating pay for 45 hours as simply 18 $\times$ 45 (ignoring the higher overtime rate for hours beyond 40) gives the same total as the correct formula.**  (false)

18 $\times$ 45 = 810, but the correct pay at 45 hours (using the overtime rate for hours 41–45) is 855. These are different totals.

**Quick check:** compare directly: flat-rate estimate = 18 $\times$ 45 = 810; correct overtime-adjusted pay = 855 — a $45 difference from skipping the rate split.
tasks.solution_overview: An employee earns $18/hour for the first 40 hours worked in a week, and time-and-a-half ($27/hour) for each hour beyond 40. Let h represent total hours worked in a week $(h > 40)$. She wants her weekly pay to be at least $850.

tasks.title: Markup vs. Profit Margin
tasks.context: A retailer buys an item for $40 (its cost) and wants to price it so that the profit margin — profit as a percentage of the selling price, $(s - 40)/s$ — is at least 20%. Let s represent the selling price.
statements: Selling at $50 gives exactly a 20% margin.
Selling at $45 gives at least a 20% margin.
Pricing the item with a 20% markup on cost ($40 $\times$ 1.20 = $48) also satisfies the 20% margin requirement.
Selling at $60 gives a margin above 20%.
The minimum selling price needed is $50.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Selling at $50 gives exactly a 20% margin.**  (true)

$\dfrac{50−40}{50}$ = $\dfrac{10}{50}$ = 0.20 = 20% exactly.

**Quick check:** plug in $s = 50$: $\dfrac{50−40}{50}$ = 0.20.

**B) Selling at $45 gives at least a 20% margin.**  (false)

$\dfrac{45−40}{45}$ = $\dfrac{5}{45}$ ≈ 0.111 = 11.1%, which is below the 20% target.

**Quick check:** plug in $s = 45$: $\dfrac{5}{45}$ ≈ 11.1% < 20%.

**C) Pricing the item with a 20% markup on cost ($40 $\times$ 1.20 = $48) also satisfies the 20% margin requirement.**  (false)

A 20% markup on the $40 cost gives a selling price of $48. But the margin at that price is $\dfrac{48−40}{48}$ = $\dfrac{8}{48}$ ≈ 16.7%, which is below the 20% margin target.

**Quick check:** compare directly: 20% markup on cost gives price $48 and margin ≈16.7%; but a true 20% margin requires price $50 — the two percentages point to different prices.

**D) Selling at $60 gives a margin above 20%.**  (true)

$\dfrac{60−40}{60}$ = $\dfrac{20}{60}$ ≈ 0.333 = 33.3%, which is above 20%.

**Quick check:** plug in $s = 60$: $\dfrac{20}{60}$ ≈ 33.3% > 20%.

**E) The minimum selling price needed is $50.**  (true)

Since s represents a price, $s > 0$, so multiplying both sides of $(s - 40)/s \ge 0.20$ by s doesn't flip the inequality: $s - 40 \ge 0.20s$

${0.80s \ge 40}$

$s \ge 50$.
tasks.solution_overview: A retailer buys an item for $40 (its cost) and wants to price it so that the profit margin — profit as a percentage of the selling price, $(s - 40)/s$ — is at least 20%. Let s represent the selling price.

tasks.title: Currency Conversion Budget
tasks.context: A traveler converts euros to US dollars at a rate of $1.08 per €1, with a flat $15 conversion fee subtracted after the exchange. Let E represent the number of euros converted (a whole number). She wants to receive at least $500 USD.
statements: Converting 477 euros results in at least $500 USD.
Converting 476 euros results in at least $500 USD.
The minimum whole number of euros needed is 476.
Converting 500 euros results in more than $520 USD.
The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as ${1.08E - 15 \ge 500}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Converting 477 euros results in at least $500 USD.**  (true)

1.08(477) - 15 = 515.16 - 15 = 500.16, which is at least $500.

**Quick check:** plug in $E = 477$: 1.08(477) - 15 = 500.16 $\ge$ 500.

**B) Converting 476 euros results in at least $500 USD.**  (false)

1.08(476) - 15 = 514.08 - 15 = 499.08, which is below $500.

**Quick check:** plug in $E = 476$: 1.08(476) - 15 = 499.08 < 500.

**C) The minimum whole number of euros needed is 476.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${1.08E - 15 \ge 500}$ gives $E \ge 476.85$. Since 476 euros falls short (only $499.08), the minimum whole number of euros is 477, not 476.

**D) Converting 500 euros results in more than $520 USD.**  (true)

1.08(500) - 15 = 540 - 15 = 525, which is more than $520.

**Quick check:** plug in $E = 500$: 1.08(500) - 15 = 525 > 520.

**E) The inequality modeling this situation is correctly written as ${1.08E - 15 \ge 500}$.**  (true)

The converted amount is ${1.08E}$, and the flat $15 fee is subtracted after conversion, so the total must be at least $500: ${1.08E - 15 \ge 500}$.
tasks.solution_overview: A traveler converts euros to US dollars at a rate of $1.08 per €1, with a flat $15 conversion fee subtracted after the exchange. Let E represent the number of euros converted (a whole number). She wants to receive at least $500 USD.

tasks.title: Food Truck Break-Even
tasks.context: A food truck has fixed daily costs of $150. Each item sold costs $3 in ingredients and sells for $8. Let x represent the number of items sold in a day. The owner wants a daily profit of at least $200.
statements: Selling 70 items results in a profit of exactly $200.
Selling 65 items results in a profit of at least $200.
The break-even point (profit = $0) occurs at more items sold than the $200 profit target.
Selling 100 items results in a profit greater than $300.
The minimum number of items needed to reach the profit goal is 70.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Selling 70 items results in a profit of exactly $200.**  (true)

Profit = ${8x - (150+3x) = 5x - 150}$. At $x = 70$: 5(70)-150 = 350-150 = 200 exactly.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 70$: 5(70) - 150 = 200.

**B) Selling 65 items results in a profit of at least $200.**  (false)

At $x = 65$: 5(65)-150 = 325-150 = 175, which is below $200.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 65$: 5(65) - 150 = 175 < 200.

**C) The break-even point (profit = $0) occurs at more items sold than the $200 profit target.**  (false)

The break-even point solves ${5x - 150 = 0}$, giving $x = 30$. Since 30 is less than 70 (the $200-profit target), break-even actually occurs at fewer items sold, not more.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 30$ into the profit formula: 5(30)-150 = 0, confirming break-even at 30 items, well below the 70 needed for $200 profit.

**D) Selling 100 items results in a profit greater than $300.**  (true)

At $x = 100$: 5(100)-150 = 500-150 = 350, which is more than $300.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 100$: 5(100) - 150 = 350 > 300.

**E) The minimum number of items needed to reach the profit goal is 70.**  (true)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${5x - 150 \ge 200}$ gives $x \ge 70$, matching the minimum number of items.
tasks.solution_overview: A food truck has fixed daily costs of $150. Each item sold costs $3 in ingredients and sells for $8. Let x represent the number of items sold in a day. The owner wants a daily profit of at least $200.

tasks.title: Manufacturing Tolerance Inspection
tasks.context: A metal rod passes inspection only if both conditions hold at once: its diameter d (mm) must satisfy $|d - 12| \le 0.3$, and its weight w (grams) must be strictly less than ${50g}$.
statements: A rod with d = 12.2mm and w = ${45g}$ passes inspection.
A rod with d = 12.4mm and w = ${40g}$ passes inspection.
A rod with d = 11.7mm and w = ${52g}$ passes inspection.
A rod with d = 12.3mm and w = ${30g}$ passes inspection.
A rod with d = 12.3mm and w = ${50g}$ passes inspection.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A rod with d = 12.2mm and w = ${45g}$ passes inspection.**  (true)

$|12.2-12| = 0.2 \le 0.3$, so the diameter is within tolerance; and 45 < 50, so the weight also passes. Both conditions hold.

**Quick check:** check both: diameter deviation = 0.2 (within 0.3), weight = 45 (under 50) — both pass.

**B) A rod with d = 12.4mm and w = ${40g}$ passes inspection.**  (false)

$|12.4-12| = 0.4$, which exceeds the 0.3 tolerance — the rod fails on diameter alone, regardless of its weight.

**Quick check:** check diameter alone: deviation = 0.4 > 0.3, already a fail.

**C) A rod with d = 11.7mm and w = ${52g}$ passes inspection.**  (false)

$|11.7-12| = 0.3 \le 0.3$, so the diameter is exactly at the boundary and still passes (the diameter condition uses “ $\le$ ”). But w = 52 is not less than 50, so the rod fails on weight.

**Quick check:** check both: diameter deviation = 0.3 (boundary, passes since $\le$ ); weight = 52 (fails since not < 50) — overall fail.

**D) A rod with d = 12.3mm and w = ${30g}$ passes inspection.**  (true)

$|12.3-12| = 0.3 \le 0.3$, diameter passes (boundary included); w = 30 < 50, weight passes. Both conditions hold.

**Quick check:** check both: diameter deviation = 0.3 (boundary, passes); weight = 30 (passes) — overall pass.

**E) A rod with d = 12.3mm and w = ${50g}$ passes inspection.**  (false)

$|12.3-12| = 0.3 \le 0.3$, so the diameter passes (its boundary is included, using “ $\le$ ”). But w = 50 is not strictly less than 50, so the weight condition fails at its own boundary.
tasks.solution_overview: A metal rod passes inspection only if both conditions hold at once: its diameter d (mm) must satisfy $|d - 12| \le 0.3$, and its weight w (grams) must be strictly less than ${50g}$.

tasks.title: Tiered Shipping Rates
tasks.context: A shipping company charges a flat $8 for packages weighing 10kg or less. For packages over 10kg (up to 20kg), it charges $8 plus $0.50 per kg over 10. Let w represent the package weight in kg. A customer wants the shipping cost to be $12 or less.
statements: A package weighing 5kg costs $8, which is within the $12 budget.
A package weighing 15kg stays within the $12 budget.
A package weighing 18kg costs exactly $12.
A package weighing 19kg stays within the $12 budget.
Applying the second bracket's formula, ${8 + 0.5(w - 10)}$, to a 5kg package gives the same $8 cost as correctly using the flat-rate bracket.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A package weighing 5kg costs $8, which is within the $12 budget.**  (true)

At w=5kg (in the 0–10kg bracket), the cost is a flat $8, which is within the $12 budget.

**Quick check:** w = 5 falls in the flat-rate bracket: cost = $8 $\le$ $12.

**B) A package weighing 15kg stays within the $12 budget.**  (true)

At w=15kg (in the over-10kg bracket): 8 + 0.5(15-10) = 8+2.5 = 10.5, within the $12 budget.

**Quick check:** plug in w = 15: 8 + 0.5(5) = 10.5 $\le$ 12.

**C) A package weighing 18kg costs exactly $12.**  (true)

At w=18kg: 8 + 0.5(18-10) = 8+4 = 12, exactly at the budget limit.

**Quick check:** plug in w = 18: 8 + 0.5(8) = 12.

**D) A package weighing 19kg stays within the $12 budget.**  (false)

At w=19kg: 8 + 0.5(19-10) = 8+4.5 = 12.5, which is over the $12 budget.

**Quick check:** plug in w = 19: 8 + 0.5(9) = 12.5 > 12.

**E) Applying the second bracket's formula, ${8 + 0.5(w - 10)}$, to a 5kg package gives the same $8 cost as correctly using the flat-rate bracket.**  (false)

Plugging w=5 into the second bracket's formula gives 8 + 0.5(5-10) = 8 + 0.5(-5) = 8-2.5 = 5.5, which does not match the correct flat-rate cost of $8.
tasks.solution_overview: A shipping company charges a flat $8 for packages weighing 10kg or less. For packages over 10kg (up to 20kg), it charges $8 plus $0.50 per kg over 10. Let w represent the package weight in kg. A customer wants the shipping cost to be $12 or less.

tasks.title: Support Cable Length
tasks.context: A support cable runs from a fixed point on the ground, 20 meters horizontally from the base of a pole, up to an attachment point at height h meters on the pole. The cable length is $L = \sqrt{h^{2} + 20^{2}}$. Engineers require the cable length to be at most 25 meters, with $h \ge 0$.
statements: A height of 15m results in a cable length of exactly 25m.
A height of 10m results in a cable length under 25m.
A height of 16m keeps the cable length at or under 25m.
Squaring both sides of $\sqrt{h^{2}+400} \le 25$ to get $h^{2}+400 \le 625$ is valid here because both sides of the original inequality are guaranteed non-negative.
Since there's a square root in this inequality, squaring both sides is always a safe step, regardless of the signs involved, with no additional check ever needed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A height of 15m results in a cable length of exactly 25m.**  (true)

$\sqrt{15^{2}+20^{2}} = \sqrt{225+400} = \sqrt{625} = 25$, exactly at the limit.

**Quick check:** plug in $h = 15$: $\sqrt{225+400} = \sqrt{625} = 25$.

**B) A height of 10m results in a cable length under 25m.**  (true)

$\sqrt{10^{2}+400} = \sqrt{500} \approx 22.36$, which is under 25m.

**Quick check:** plug in $h = 10$: $\sqrt{100+400} = \sqrt{500} \approx 22.4 < 25$.

**C) A height of 16m keeps the cable length at or under 25m.**  (false)

$\sqrt{16^{2}+400} = \sqrt{656} \approx 25.61$, which is over 25m.

**Quick check:** plug in $h = 16$: $\sqrt{256+400} = \sqrt{656} \approx 25.6 > 25$.

**D) Squaring both sides of $\sqrt{h^{2}+400} \le 25$ to get $h^{2}+400 \le 625$ is valid here because both sides of the original inequality are guaranteed non-negative.**  (true)

Squaring is a reversible, direction-preserving step only when both sides being compared are non-negative. Here, a cable length is always $\ge$ 0, and 25 is also $\ge$ 0, so squaring both sides of $\sqrt{h^{2}+400} \le 25$ correctly gives $h^{2}+400 \le 625$ without flipping or distorting the inequality.

**E) Since there's a square root in this inequality, squaring both sides is always a safe step, regardless of the signs involved, with no additional check ever needed.**  (false)

Squaring both sides only works safely when both sides are known to be non-negative. If the right-hand side of an inequality could be negative, squaring can introduce false solutions or lose valid ones — it is not a universally safe operation just because a square root happens to be present.

**Common trap:** It's tempting to treat “square both sides to remove a square root” as a rule that always applies. It only works cleanly here because a cable length and the number 25 are both guaranteed non-negative in this specific scenario — in general, squaring an inequality with a variable (possibly negative) expression on either side requires checking signs first, or it can produce an incorrect solution set.
tasks.solution_overview: A support cable runs from a fixed point on the ground, 20 meters horizontally from the base of a pole, up to an attachment point at height h meters on the pole. The cable length is $L = \sqrt{h^{2} + 20^{2}}$. Engineers require the cable length to be at most 25 meters, with $h \ge 0$.

tasks.title: Comparing Three Internet Plans
tasks.context: Three internet plans are available. Plan A: $30/month flat. Plan B: $10/month plus $0.05 per GB used. Plan C: $20/month plus $0.02 per GB used. Let g represent GB used per month.
statements: At 200 GB of usage, Plan B is the cheapest of the three.
At 400 GB of usage, Plan A is the cheapest of the three.
At 600 GB of usage, Plan A is the cheapest of the three.
Plan B is never the most expensive of the three plans, regardless of usage.
There exists a usage level at which all three plans cost exactly the same amount.
tactical_explanations:
**A) At 200 GB of usage, Plan B is the cheapest of the three.**  (true)

At $g = 200$: A=$30, B=10+0.05(200)=$20, C=20+0.02(200)=$24. Plan B is the lowest.

**Quick check:** plug in $g = 200$ into all three: A=30, B=20, $C = 24$ — B is lowest.

**B) At 400 GB of usage, Plan A is the cheapest of the three.**  (false)

At $g = 400$: A=$30, B=10+0.05(400)=$30, C=20+0.02(400)=$28. Plan C is actually the lowest, not Plan A.

**Quick check:** plug in $g = 400$ into all three: A=30, B=30, $C = 28$ — C is lowest, not A.

**C) At 600 GB of usage, Plan A is the cheapest of the three.**  (true)

At $g = 600$: A=$30, B=10+0.05(600)=$40, C=20+0.02(600)=$32. Plan A is the lowest.

**Quick check:** plug in $g = 600$ into all three: A=30, B=40, $C = 32$ — A is lowest.

**D) Plan B is never the most expensive of the three plans, regardless of usage.**  (false)

At $g = 600$ (from part C), Plan B costs $40, which is actually the highest of the three plans at that usage level $(A = 30, C = 32, B = 40)$. So Plan B does become the most expensive option once usage is high enough.

**E) There exists a usage level at which all three plans cost exactly the same amount.**  (false)

Plan A equals Plan B at $g = 400$ (both $30), Plan A equals Plan C at $g = 500$ (both $30), and Plan B equals Plan C at $g \approx 333.3$ (both ≈$26.67) — three different crossover points, none of which is shared by all three plans at once.
tasks.solution_overview: Three internet plans are available. Plan A: $30/month flat. Plan B: $10/month plus $0.05 per GB used. Plan C: $20/month plus $0.02 per GB used. Let g represent GB used per month.

tasks.title: College GPA with Credit-Hour Weights
tasks.context: A student's GPA is a weighted average of course grade points, weighted by credit hours. She has completed a 3-credit course (3.0 grade points) and a 4-credit course (2.7 grade points). She is now taking a 3-credit course and wants her overall GPA across all 10 credits to be at least 3.0. Let x represent the grade points she earns in the new course (maximum possible is 4.0).
statements: Earning 3.4 grade points in the new course meets her GPA goal exactly.
Earning 3.2 grade points in the new course meets her GPA goal.
The minimum grade points she needs in the new course is 3.0.
Since the maximum possible grade points in a single course is 4.0, it is possible for her to reach her GPA goal.

This problem uses credit hours as weights, similar in structure to Question 16's percentage weights for homework/midterm/final — except here the weights are the number of credits each course is worth.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Earning 3.4 grade points in the new course meets her GPA goal exactly.**  (true)

Weighted sum from completed courses: 3(3.0)+4(2.7) = 9+10.8 = 19.8. Total credits = 3+4+3 = 10. $\dfrac{19.8+3x}{10}$ $\ge$ 3.0

${19.8+3x \ge 30}$

$x \ge 3.4$. At $x = 3.4$, the GPA is exactly 3.0.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 3.4$: (19.8+3(3.4))/10 = $\dfrac{19.8+10.2}{10}$ = $\dfrac{30}{10}$ = 3.0.

**B) Earning 3.2 grade points in the new course meets her GPA goal.**  (false)

At $x = 3.2$: (19.8+3(3.2))/10 = $\dfrac{19.8+9.6}{10}$ = $\dfrac{29.4}{10}$ = 2.94, below the 3.0 goal.

**Quick check:** plug in $x = 3.2$: total=29.4, GPA=2.94 < 3.0.

**C) The minimum grade points she needs in the new course is 3.0.**  (false)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. the inequality gives $x \ge 3.4$, meaning the grade points needed in the new course is 3.4 — not 3.0.

**D) Since the maximum possible grade points in a single course is 4.0, it is possible for her to reach her GPA goal.**  (true)

Since the required grade points $(x \ge 3.4)$ is below the maximum possible (4.0), the goal is achievable — there is a valid range of grades (3.4 to 4.0) that would work.

**E) This problem uses credit hours as weights, similar in structure to Question 16's percentage weights for homework/midterm/final — except here the weights are the number of credits each course is worth.**  (true)

Both problems compute a weighted average as (sum of value $\times$ weight for each item) ÷ (total weight) $\ge$ target. In Question 16 the weights were percentages of the total grade; here the weights are credit hours, but the algebraic structure is identical.
tasks.solution_overview: A student's GPA is a weighted average of course grade points, weighted by credit hours. She has completed a 3-credit course (3.0 grade points) and a 4-credit course (2.7 grade points). She is now taking a 3-credit course and wants her overall GPA across all 10 credits to be at least 3.0. Let x represent the grade points she earns in the new course (maximum possible is 4.0).

tasks.title: Chained Discount, Tax, and Coupon
tasks.context: A store applies a 20% discount to an item's original price p, then adds 8% sales tax on the discounted price, then subtracts a flat $5 loyalty coupon at the very end. The final price is ${0.8p \times 1.08 - 5 = 0.864p - 5}$. A customer wants the final price to be $70 or less.
statements: An original price of $86 keeps the final price at or under $70.
An original price of $87 keeps the final price at or under $70.
The maximum original price, to the nearest whole dollar, that keeps the final price at or under $70 is $86.
Subtracting the $5 coupon before applying the discount and tax — that is, $(p - 5) \times 0.8 \times 1.08$ — would produce the same final price for a given original price.
The correctly combined formula for “discount, then tax, then coupon” is ${0.8p \times 1.08 - 5}$, which simplifies to ${0.864p - 5}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A) An original price of $86 keeps the final price at or under $70.**  (true)

0.864(86) - 5 = 74.304 - 5 = 69.304, which is at or under $70.

**Quick check:** plug in $p = 86$: 0.864(86)-5 = 69.304 $\le$ 70.

**B) An original price of $87 keeps the final price at or under $70.**  (false)

0.864(87) - 5 = 75.168 - 5 = 70.168, which is over $70.

**Quick check:** plug in $p = 87$: 0.864(87)-5 = 70.168 > 70.

**C) The maximum original price, to the nearest whole dollar, that keeps the final price at or under $70 is $86.**  (true)

**Solve**

Set up and solve. ${0.864p - 5 \le 70}$ gives $p \le 86.8056$. The largest whole dollar amount at or below this boundary is $86.

**D) Subtracting the $5 coupon before applying the discount and tax — that is, $(p - 5) \times 0.8 \times 1.08$ — would produce the same final price for a given original price.**  (false)

**Order of operations**

Applying the coupon first: (86-5) $\times$ 0.8 $\times$ 1.08 = 81 $\times$ 0.864 = 69.984. This differs from the correct-order result at the same price, $69.304, so the two orders do not produce the same final price.

**Common trap:** With three sequential operations — a percentage discount, a percentage tax, and a flat coupon — the order matters even more than with just two operations, since moving any one step changes which base amount each percentage is calculated from. Always apply the operations in the exact sequence the problem describes.

**Quick check:** compare directly at $p = 86$: correct order (discount, tax, then coupon) gives 69.304; coupon-first order gives 69.984 — a real difference for the same original price.

**E) The correctly combined formula for “discount, then tax, then coupon” is ${0.8p \times 1.08 - 5}$, which simplifies to ${0.864p - 5}$.**  (true)

The discount is applied first $(0.8p)$, then tax on the discounted amount ( $\times$ 1.08), then the flat coupon is subtracted last (-5), giving ${0.8p \times 1.08-5 = 0.864p - 5}$.
tasks.solution_overview: A store applies a 20% discount to an item's original price p, then adds 8% sales tax on the discounted price, then subtracts a flat $5 loyalty coupon at the very end. The final price is ${0.8p \times 1.08 - 5 = 0.864p - 5}$. A customer wants the final price to be $70 or less.
